source("code/erp_template.R")           # signal template
meanpower <- scan("code/meanpower.txt") # noise power spectrum

1 Introduction

The simulation notebook estimates onsets from nine separate univariate tests, one per electrode, corrects across the whole electrode-by-time space, and then reduces nine onsets to one with a minimum, a quantile or a median. The alternative developed here reverses that order: the nine electrodes are tested together, and a single onset follows directly.

The test is Hotelling’s two-sample T-squared (Hotelling, 1931), the multivariate generalisation of the t-test. At each time point the observation for one trial is not a number but a vector of nine values, one per electrode, and the test asks whether the mean vector differs between the two conditions. The result is one T-squared value per time point: a single time course, which the onset methods from the simulation notebook can then be applied to unchanged.

This differs from the virtual-electrode approach used in simulation.qmd, following Rousselet (2025), although both reduce nine electrodes to one time course. The virtual electrode takes the largest squared t across electrodes, reporting the single strongest effect and discarding the rest. Hotelling’s T-squared combines all nine, weighted by their covariance, so an effect spread thinly across several electrodes can contribute even where no single electrode is convincing alone. Whether that helps in this design is not obvious in advance, for the reasons set out in the discussion.

The notebook is deliberately kept focused: build the statistic, verify it against a published implementation, examine the time course it produces, and estimate onsets from it with the same three families of method used in simulation.qmd. Performance is then evaluated from the completed 10,000-iteration multivariate simulation.

2 Quick checks

2.1 Description

The pieces the simulation needs are rebuilt, using the same signal template and noise generator as the other notebooks (Rousselet, 2025), and the T-squared function is then checked in two ways: against DescTools::HotellingsT2Test, and against the univariate case, where a one-electrode Hotelling T-squared must equal the squared t value from a pooled-variance t-test.

2.2 Justification

The T-squared function is new code, and an error in it would propagate silently: every onset that follows would be wrong in the same way, and the figures would still look plausible. Two checks are therefore run before anything is interpreted, one against an independent implementation and one against a case whose answer is known algebraically.

2.3 Code

Code 
# variance of each row (time point) of a time x trials matrix
rowVars <- function(X){
  n <- ncol(X); m <- rowMeans(X)
  (rowSums(X^2) - n * m^2) / (n - 1)
}

# two-sample Hotelling T2 at every time point.
# A, B are time x trial x electrode arrays: one test, not nine.
hotelling_t2 <- function(A, B){
  nf <- dim(A)[1]; nA <- dim(A)[2]; nB <- dim(B)[2]; p <- dim(A)[3]
  if(p >= nA + nB - 1)
    stop("too few trials for ", p, " electrodes: the pooled covariance is singular")
  const <- (nA * nB) / (nA + nB)
  t2 <- numeric(nf)
  for(k in seq_len(nf)){
    Xa <- matrix(A[k, , ], nrow = nA)
    Xb <- matrix(B[k, , ], nrow = nB)
    d  <- colMeans(Xb) - colMeans(Xa)
    S  <- ((nA - 1) * cov(Xa) + (nB - 1) * cov(Xb)) / (nA + nB - 2)
    t2[k] <- tryCatch(const * as.numeric(crossprod(d, solve(S, d))),
                      error = function(e) NA_real_)
  }
  t2
}

# p-value for a T2 value, through its exact F transformation
hotelling_p <- function(t2, nA, nB, p){
  f <- t2 * (nA + nB - p - 1) / ((nA + nB - 2) * p)
  pf(f, df1 = p, df2 = nA + nB - p - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
}

Nt   <- 50                                    # trials per condition
w    <- c(0, 0, 0.3, 0.75, 1, 0.75, 0.3, 0, 0)
elec <- 1:9
Nf   <- length(Xf)
signal_9 <- outer(temp2, w)                   # 251 time points x 9 electrodes
colnames(signal_9) <- paste0("E", elec)

# one simulated experiment, as time x trial x electrode arrays
make_experiment <- function(){
  A <- array(0, dim = c(Nf, Nt, 9))   # condition A: noise only
  B <- array(0, dim = c(Nf, Nt, 9))   # condition B: signal + noise
  for(e in 1:9){
    A[, , e] <- replicate(Nt, eeg_noise(Nf, 500, 1, meanpower))
    B[, , e] <- replicate(Nt, signal_9[, e] + eeg_noise(Nf, 500, 1, meanpower))
  }
  list(A = A, B = B)
}

set.seed(7)
ex <- make_experiment()

# check 2: with one electrode, T2 must equal the pooled-variance squared t
a1 <- ex$A[, , 5, drop = FALSE]
b1 <- ex$B[, , 5, drop = FALSE]
t2_uni <- hotelling_t2(a1, b1)

mA <- rowMeans(ex$A[, , 5]); mB <- rowMeans(ex$B[, , 5])
vA <- rowVars(ex$A[, , 5]);  vB <- rowVars(ex$B[, , 5])
vp <- ((Nt - 1) * vA + (Nt - 1) * vB) / (2 * Nt - 2)
t2_pooled <- (mB - mA)^2 / (vp * (1 / Nt + 1 / Nt))

max(abs(t2_uni - t2_pooled))   # expect a value near zero
[1] 1.421085e-14

2.4 Observations

Both checks pass. The F statistic from hotelling_t2() and from DescTools::HotellingsT2Test agree at 2.833633, and in the one-electrode case the largest discrepancy from the pooled-variance squared t is 1.4e-14, which is machine precision. The statistic behaves as intended and the onsets below can be read.

3 The T-squared time course

3.1 Description

With the statistic verified, T-squared is computed at all 251 time points of the same simulated experiment used for the checks above, and plotted beside the virtual electrode from simulation.qmd, the maximum squared t across electrodes. The two are on different scales, so each is shown as a proportion of its own maximum.

3.2 Justification

The shape of the curve that the onset methods will be given is examined before any onset is estimated. The quantity of interest is the baseline: how flat each curve is before 160 ms, and how sharply it leaves that baseline, since a statistic with a noisier baseline produces earlier false onsets whichever method reads it.

Scaling each curve by its own maximum makes the shapes comparable, but it also limits what the comparison can settle. Flatness then means flatness relative to the peak, so a statistic with a large peak appears to have a quiet baseline even where its absolute variability is high. What matters operationally is each curve’s baseline relative to its own null distribution, which is what the permutation threshold and the FDR correction in the next section address directly. This figure is therefore read as evidence about shape, not as a verdict on either method.

3.3 Code

Code 
t2_mv <- hotelling_t2(ex$A, ex$B)

# the univariate comparison needs the Welch test from simulation.qmd
welch_t2p <- function(Ae, Be){
  nA <- ncol(Ae); nB <- ncol(Be)
  mA <- rowMeans(Ae); mB <- rowMeans(Be)
  vA <- rowVars(Ae);  vB <- rowVars(Be)
  se2  <- vA / nA + vB / nB
  tval <- (mB - mA) / sqrt(se2)
  df   <- se2^2 / ((vA / nA)^2 / (nA - 1) + (vB / nB)^2 / (nB - 1))
  list(t2 = tval^2, p = 2 * pt(-abs(tval), df))
}

# squared t at each electrode, then the maximum
T2obs <- sapply(1:9, function(e) welch_t2p(ex$A[, , e], ex$B[, , e])$t2)
t2_virtual <- apply(T2obs, 1, max)

curves <- tibble(time = Xf,
                 `Hotelling T2 (9 electrodes)` = t2_mv / max(t2_mv, na.rm = TRUE),
                 `max squared t (virtual electrode)` = t2_virtual / max(t2_virtual)) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "statistic", values_to = "value")

3.4 Figure

Code 
ggplot(curves, aes(time, value, linetype = statistic)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#ffffff") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_onset, linetype = "longdash", colour = "#c7c7c7", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(
    "Hotelling T2 (9 electrodes)" = "solid",
    "max squared t (virtual electrode)" = "longdash"

  theme_dark_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

3.5 Observations

Both statistics remain low through the pre-onset window and rise steeply after it, peaking near the peak of the template at 250 ms. Neither baseline is visibly quieter than the other on this scaling, which is the limitation set out above: the comparison is of shape, and the operative question is each curve against its own null distribution. The next section addresses that directly.

4 Onsets from the T-squared curve

4.1 Description

The curve is a single time course, so the three families of method from simulation.qmd apply directly, with no summary across electrodes needed:

  • FDR, Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli, across time points, using the exact F transformation of T-squared to obtain a p-value at each time point, then the first significant point.
  • MAX correction, taking the 95th percentile of the permutation distribution of the largest T-squared across time, then the first crossing.
  • change point on the T-squared curve, by binary segmentation as implemented in the changepoint package (Killick & Eckley, 2014).

4.2 Justification

The search space has shrunk. In simulation.qmd the FDR and MAX corrections cover 251 time points times nine electrodes; here the electrodes are inside the statistic, so the correction covers 251 time points only, and a smaller search space means a less severe correction. That gain is not free: the multivariate statistic spends nine degrees of freedom where a single electrode spends one, so its sensitivity at any given time point is lower than that of the strongest electrode. Which effect dominates is an empirical question.

The permutation is also harder to get wrong. In the univariate case one shared shuffle has to be applied deliberately across all electrodes, since electrodes are correlated and the resampling must not break that structure. Here a trial is a nine-element vector, so permuting trial labels moves the whole vector at once and the structure is preserved by construction.

Benjamini-Yekutieli is reported alongside Benjamini-Hochberg for the same reason as in simulation.qmd: adjacent time points are strongly dependent, and BY remains valid under arbitrary dependence where BH does not.

4.3 Code

Code 
nperm       <- 1000      # permutations for the MAX threshold, low on purpose:
                        # see the note on cost below
cpd_penalty <- "MBIC"   # change point penalty
sig_level   <- 0.05     # significance level for the FDR methods

# helpers that turn a time course into an onset in ms
cp_onset <- function(series, penalty = cpd_penalty){
  tryCatch({
    cp  <- cpt.meanvar(series, method = "BinSeg", Q = 2, penalty = penalty, minseglen = 2)
    pts <- cpts(cp)
    # earliest of the two change points, whatever order cpts() returns them in
    if(length(pts) == 0) NA_real_ else Xf[min(pts)]
  }, error = function(e) NA_real_)
}
first_cross <- function(series, thr){
  s <- which(series > thr); if(length(s) == 0) NA_real_ else Xf[s[1]]
}
first_sig <- function(pcol, level = sig_level){
  s <- which(pcol < level); if(length(s) == 0) NA_real_ else Xf[s[1]]
}

# onsets from one T2 curve, given the arrays it came from
mv_onsets <- function(A, B, nperm = nperm){
  nf <- dim(A)[1]; nA <- dim(A)[2]; nB <- dim(B)[2]; p <- dim(A)[3]

  t2 <- hotelling_t2(A, B)
  pv <- hotelling_p(t2, nA, nB, p)

  # permutation null: shuffle trial labels, keeping each trial's nine values
  # together, and save the largest T2 across time
  pool <- array(0, dim = c(nf, nA + nB, p))
  pool[, 1:nA, ]              <- A
  pool[, (nA + 1):(nA + nB), ] <- B

  null_max <- numeric(nperm)
  for(b in 1:nperm){
    perm <- sample(nA + nB)
    null_max[b] <- max(hotelling_t2(pool[, perm[1:nA], , drop = FALSE],
                                    pool[, perm[(nA + 1):(nA + nB)], , drop = FALSE]),
                       na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  thr <- quantile(null_max, 0.95, names = FALSE)

  tibble(method = c("Hotelling FDR BH", "Hotelling FDR BY",
                    "Hotelling MAX", "Hotelling CPD"),
         onset  = c(first_sig(p.adjust(pv, "BH")),
                    first_sig(p.adjust(pv, "BY")),
                    first_cross(t2, thr),
                    cp_onset(t2)))
}

4.4 Table

Code 
set.seed(11)
mv_onsets(ex$A, ex$B, nperm = nperm) |> knitr::kable()

4.5 Observations

On this run Benjamini-Hochberg returns 2 ms, the first time point of the epoch, which is a false positive rather than an estimate. Benjamini-Yekutieli gives 194 ms, the MAX threshold 204 ms and change point 178 ms, all later than the true 160 ms. Benjamini-Yekutieli is later than Benjamini-Hochberg, as its more conservative correction implies.

4.6 Worked example

The four multivariate estimators can be read from the same Hotelling T-squared time course.

Code 
t2_ex_nb <- hotelling_t2(ex$A, ex$B)
p_ex_nb <- hotelling_p(t2_ex_nb, dim(ex$A)[2], dim(ex$B)[2], dim(ex$A)[3])
bh_ex_nb <- p.adjust(p_ex_nb, "BH")
by_ex_nb <- p.adjust(p_ex_nb, "BY")

set.seed(2604)
nA_nb <- dim(ex$A)[2]
nB_nb <- dim(ex$B)[2]
pool_nb <- array(0, dim = c(length(Xf), nA_nb + nB_nb, 9))
pool_nb[, 1:nA_nb, ] <- ex$A
pool_nb[, (nA_nb + 1):(nA_nb + nB_nb), ] <- ex$B
null_nb <- numeric(nperm)
for(b in seq_len(nperm)){
  perm <- sample(nA_nb + nB_nb)
  null_nb[b] <- max(
    hotelling_t2(
      pool_nb[, perm[1:nA_nb], , drop = FALSE],
      pool_nb[, perm[(nA_nb + 1):(nA_nb + nB_nb)], , drop = FALSE]
    ),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}
thr_nb <- quantile(null_nb, 0.95, names = FALSE)

methods_nb <- c("Hotelling BH", "Hotelling BY", "Hotelling MAX", "Hotelling CPD")
onsets_nb <- tibble(
  method = factor(methods_nb, levels = methods_nb),
  onset = c(
    first_sig(bh_ex_nb),
    first_sig(by_ex_nb),
    first_cross(t2_ex_nb, thr_nb),
    cp_onset(t2_ex_nb)
  )
)

trace_nb <- crossing(
  tibble(time = Xf, t2 = t2_ex_nb),
  method = factor(methods_nb, levels = methods_nb)
)

sig_nb <- bind_rows(
  tibble(time = Xf[bh_ex_nb < sig_level], method = "Hotelling BH"),
  tibble(time = Xf[by_ex_nb < sig_level], method = "Hotelling BY")
) |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = methods_nb),
         y = -0.05 * max(t2_ex_nb, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(trace_nb, aes(time, t2)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#ffffff", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(
    data = sig_nb,
    aes(x = time - 1, xend = time + 1, y = y, yend = y),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#ffffff",
    linewidth = 1.7, lineend = "butt"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    data = tibble(method = factor("Hotelling MAX", levels = methods_nb),
                  threshold = thr_nb),
    aes(yintercept = threshold), colour = "#c7c7c7",
    linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_onset, colour = "#c7c7c7",
             linetype = "longdash", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(
    data = onsets_nb |> filter(!is.na(onset)),
    aes(xintercept = onset), colour = "#ffffff",
    linetype = "solid", linewidth = 0.75
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~method, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.10, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = "Time (ms)", y = expression(T^2)) +
  theme_dark_bw() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(colour = "#ffffff", face = "bold"))

5 Simulation results (10,000 iterations)

5.1 Description

One experiment says little, so performance is evaluated over 10,000 Monte Carlo iterations with 50 trials per condition. The completed simulation is loaded from the saved result file rather than regenerated when this notebook is rendered.

5.2 Justification

Using the saved production run keeps the analysis reproducible without repeating the computationally expensive permutation simulation during rendering. The four methods are therefore evaluated from the same 10,000 completed multivariate experiments.

5.3 Code

Code 
# Load the completed multivariate simulation output.
mv_file <- if(file.exists("data/simres_n50_mult.RData")) {
  "data/simres_n50_mult.RData"
} else {
  "simres_n50_mult.RData"
}

load(mv_file)

# Standardise the saved result table if necessary.
if(exists("sim_mv")) {
  sim_mv <- as_tibble(sim_mv)
} else {
  objs <- mget(ls(), inherits = FALSE)
  hits <- objs[vapply(objs, function(x)
    is.data.frame(x) &&
      all(c("iter", "method", "onset") %in% names(x)), logical(1))]
  if(length(hits) != 1) stop("Could not identify the saved multivariate result table.")
  sim_mv <- as_tibble(hits[[1]])
}

stopifnot(max(sim_mv$iter, na.rm = TRUE) == 10000)

mv_methods <- c("Hotelling FDR BH", "Hotelling FDR BY",
                "Hotelling MAX", "Hotelling CPD")

sim_mv <- sim_mv |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = mv_methods))

method_summary_mv <- sim_mv |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(
    median_onset = median(onset, na.rm = TRUE),
    bias = round(median_onset - true_onset, 1),
    mae = round(mean(abs(onset - true_onset), na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    sd_onset = round(sd(onset, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    underestimation = round(100 * mean(onset < true_onset, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(onset)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Load the completed univariate main run solely for this cross-family comparison.
univ_file_nb <- if(file.exists("data/simres_n50.RData")) {
  "data/simres_n50.RData"
} else {
  "simres_n50.RData"
}

env_nb <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
load(univ_file_nb, envir = env_nb)
obj_nb <- as.list(env_nb)

pick_nb <- function(required, forbidden = character()){
  hit <- obj_nb[vapply(obj_nb, function(x)
    is.data.frame(x) &&
      all(required %in% names(x)) &&
      !any(forbidden %in% names(x)), logical(1))]
  if(length(hit) != 1) stop("Could not identify saved univariate table in ", univ_file_nb)
  as_tibble(hit[[1]])
}

pe_nb <- if("perelec_all" %in% names(obj_nb)) {
  as_tibble(obj_nb[["perelec_all"]])
} else {
  pick_nb(c("iter", "electrode", "weight", "method", "onset"))
}
vi_nb <- if("virtual_all" %in% names(obj_nb)) {
  as_tibble(obj_nb[["virtual_all"]])
} else {
  pick_nb(c("iter", "method", "onset"), c("electrode", "weight"))
}

safe_min_nb <- function(x){
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if(length(x) == 0) NA_real_ else min(x)
}
safe_q_nb <- function(x, p){
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if(length(x) == 0) NA_real_ else quantile(x, p, names = FALSE)
}

group_nb <- pe_nb |>
  group_by(iter, method) |>
  summarise(
    min = safe_min_nb(onset),
    median = safe_q_nb(onset, 0.50),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(min, median), names_to = "summary", values_to = "onset") |>
  bind_rows(vi_nb |> transmute(iter, method, summary = "single", onset))

spec_nb <- tribble(
  ~method, ~summary, ~strategy,
  "FDR BH", "min", "BH min",
  "FDR BY", "min", "BY min",
  "MAX across", "min", "MAX min",
  "CPD per electrode", "median", "CPD median",
  "CPD if MAX significant", "min", "CPD MAX-selected min",
  "CPD virtual", "single", "Pooled CPD"
)

primary_cmp_nb <- group_nb |>
  inner_join(spec_nb, by = c("method", "summary")) |>
  group_by(strategy) |>
  summarise(
    bias = median(onset, na.rm = TRUE) - true_onset,
    mae = mean(abs(onset - true_onset), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(family = "Primary methods", label = strategy)

hot_cmp_nb <- sim_mv |>
  filter(!is.na(onset)) |>

    mae = mean(abs(onset - true_onset)),

cmp_nb <- bind_rows(primary_cmp_nb, hot_cmp_nb) |>

  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(8, 14, 8, 8))

5.6 Observations

Across 10,000 simulations, Hotelling BH had the smallest median bias among the four multivariate procedures, with a median onset of 180 ms and a bias of +20 ms, but its distribution was broad: MAE was 53.5 ms, SD was 65.7 ms, and 39.7% of estimates occurred before 160 ms. Hotelling BY was later, with a median onset of 196 ms, bias of +36 ms, MAE of 41.4 ms, SD of 38.0 ms, and 8.8% underestimation. Hotelling MAX had a median onset of 202 ms and bias of +42 ms; its MAE was 43.7 ms, SD 20.8 ms, and underestimation 1.9%. Hotelling CPD gave the lowest MAE and smallest SD of the four multivariate procedures, with a median onset of 186 ms, bias of +26 ms, MAE of 26.5 ms, SD of 11.4 ms, and 1.6% underestimation. All four methods returned an onset in all 10,000 simulations.

6 Discussion and next steps

This simulation is not built to favour the multivariate test, and two features of it work directly against the test. Both belong in any reading of the results.

The first is the noise. Hotelling’s T-squared earns its advantage over separate univariate tests by using the covariance between electrodes: when the noise is correlated across electrodes but the effect is not, the test can separate the two. In this simulation the noise is generated independently at every electrode, so the true covariance matrix is close to diagonal and there is little structure for the test to exploit. What it estimates instead is sampling noise in a nine by nine matrix, from 100 trials. The design was chosen in the demo as the harder case for the univariate methods, but it is also the case in which the multivariate test has least to offer. A version with noise shared across neighbouring electrodes would be a fairer test of it, and is the obvious follow-up.

The second is dilution. Four of the nine electrodes carry no signal at all. Hotelling’s T-squared spends degrees of freedom on all nine dimensions regardless, so those four contribute variance without contributing effect, and the statistic is weaker than it would be with only the five signal electrodes. This is the same electrode-selection problem as in simulation.qmd, arriving from a different direction: there it decided which onsets to summarise, here it decides which dimensions enter the test. The remedies are the same, an a priori region of interest or a data-driven selection step, and neither is free.

Against those disadvantages sits one clear advantage: the correction covers 251 time points instead of 251 times nine, and the permutation cannot break the correlation structure, since it moves whole trials. Comparable performance in a design tilted against the test would therefore be a stronger result than the raw numbers suggest.

Next steps:

  • fold the T-squared curve into simulation.qmd as four further strategies, so that the multivariate and univariate methods are compared on the same runs rather than across notebooks.
  • repeat with noise shared across neighbouring electrodes, which is the case the multivariate test is designed for.
  • try a linear discriminant analysis across electrodes as an alternative multivariate statistic, which does not rest on a common covariance in the same way.
  • test the effect of restricting the test to a subset of electrodes, to separate the dilution problem from the noise problem.

7 References

  • Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate: A practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 57(1), 289-300. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x
  • Benjamini, Y., & Yekutieli, D. (2001). The control of the false discovery rate in multiple testing under dependency. The Annals of Statistics, 29(4), 1165-1188. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1013699998
  • Hotelling, H. (1931). The generalization of Student’s ratio. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 2(3), 360-378. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177732979
  • Killick, R., & Eckley, I. A. (2014). changepoint: An R package for changepoint analysis. Journal of Statistical Software, 58(3), 1-19. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v058.i03

# Introduction

The simulation notebook estimates onsets from nine separate univariate tests, one per electrode, corrects across the whole electrode-by-time space, and then reduces nine onsets to one with a minimum, a quantile or a median. The alternative developed here reverses that order: the nine electrodes are tested together, and a single onset follows directly.

The test is Hotelling's two-sample T-squared (Hotelling, 1931), the multivariate generalisation of the t-test. At each time point the observation for one trial is not a number but a vector of nine values, one per electrode, and the test asks whether the mean vector differs between the two conditions. The result is one T-squared value per time point: a single time course, which the onset methods from the simulation notebook can then be applied to unchanged.

This differs from the virtual-electrode approach used in `simulation.qmd`, following Rousselet (2025), although both reduce nine electrodes to one time course. The virtual electrode takes the largest squared t across electrodes, reporting the single strongest effect and discarding the rest. Hotelling's T-squared combines all nine, weighted by their covariance, so an effect spread thinly across several electrodes can contribute even where no single electrode is convincing alone. Whether that helps in this design is not obvious in advance, for the reasons set out in the discussion.

The notebook is deliberately kept focused: build the statistic, verify it against a published implementation, examine the time course it produces, and estimate onsets from it with the same three families of method used in `simulation.qmd`. Performance is then evaluated from the completed 10,000-iteration multivariate simulation.

# Quick checks

## Description

The pieces the simulation needs are rebuilt, using the same signal template and noise generator as the other notebooks (Rousselet, 2025), and the T-squared function is then checked in two ways: against `DescTools::HotellingsT2Test`, and against the univariate case, where a one-electrode Hotelling T-squared must equal the squared t value from a pooled-variance t-test.

## Justification

The T-squared function is new code, and an error in it would propagate silently: every onset that follows would be wrong in the same way, and the figures would still look plausible. Two checks are therefore run before anything is interpreted, one against an independent implementation and one against a case whose answer is known algebraically.

## Code

```{r}
# variance of each row (time point) of a time x trials matrix
rowVars <- function(X){
  n <- ncol(X); m <- rowMeans(X)
  (rowSums(X^2) - n * m^2) / (n - 1)
}

# two-sample Hotelling T2 at every time point.
# A, B are time x trial x electrode arrays: one test, not nine.
hotelling_t2 <- function(A, B){
  nf <- dim(A)[1]; nA <- dim(A)[2]; nB <- dim(B)[2]; p <- dim(A)[3]
  if(p >= nA + nB - 1)
    stop("too few trials for ", p, " electrodes: the pooled covariance is singular")
  const <- (nA * nB) / (nA + nB)
  t2 <- numeric(nf)
  for(k in seq_len(nf)){
    Xa <- matrix(A[k, , ], nrow = nA)
    Xb <- matrix(B[k, , ], nrow = nB)
    d  <- colMeans(Xb) - colMeans(Xa)
    S  <- ((nA - 1) * cov(Xa) + (nB - 1) * cov(Xb)) / (nA + nB - 2)
    t2[k] <- tryCatch(const * as.numeric(crossprod(d, solve(S, d))),
                      error = function(e) NA_real_)
  }
  t2
}

# p-value for a T2 value, through its exact F transformation
hotelling_p <- function(t2, nA, nB, p){
  f <- t2 * (nA + nB - p - 1) / ((nA + nB - 2) * p)
  pf(f, df1 = p, df2 = nA + nB - p - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
}

Nt   <- 50                                    # trials per condition
w    <- c(0, 0, 0.3, 0.75, 1, 0.75, 0.3, 0, 0)
elec <- 1:9
Nf   <- length(Xf)
signal_9 <- outer(temp2, w)                   # 251 time points x 9 electrodes
colnames(signal_9) <- paste0("E", elec)

# one simulated experiment, as time x trial x electrode arrays
make_experiment <- function(){
  A <- array(0, dim = c(Nf, Nt, 9))   # condition A: noise only
  B <- array(0, dim = c(Nf, Nt, 9))   # condition B: signal + noise
  for(e in 1:9){
    A[, , e] <- replicate(Nt, eeg_noise(Nf, 500, 1, meanpower))
    B[, , e] <- replicate(Nt, signal_9[, e] + eeg_noise(Nf, 500, 1, meanpower))
  }
  list(A = A, B = B)
}

set.seed(7)
ex <- make_experiment()

dim(ex$A)            # expect 251 x 50 x 9
true_onset           # expect 160 ms
```

```{r}
# check 1: against DescTools at a single time point after the onset
t_idx <- which.min(abs(Xf - 200))   # a time point well after the onset
t2_mine <- hotelling_t2(ex$A[t_idx, , , drop = FALSE], ex$B[t_idx, , , drop = FALSE])

# DescTools reports the F statistic, so convert mine the same way
f_mine <- t2_mine * (2 * Nt - 9 - 1) / ((2 * Nt - 2) * 9)

if(requireNamespace("DescTools", quietly = TRUE)){
  ref <- DescTools::HotellingsT2Test(matrix(ex$B[t_idx, , ], nrow = Nt),
                                     matrix(ex$A[t_idx, , ], nrow = Nt))
  tibble(source = c("hotelling_t2()", "DescTools"),
         F      = c(f_mine, as.numeric(ref$statistic))) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 6)
} else {
  message("DescTools not installed: skipping the external check")
}
```

```{r}
# check 2: with one electrode, T2 must equal the pooled-variance squared t
a1 <- ex$A[, , 5, drop = FALSE]
b1 <- ex$B[, , 5, drop = FALSE]
t2_uni <- hotelling_t2(a1, b1)

mA <- rowMeans(ex$A[, , 5]); mB <- rowMeans(ex$B[, , 5])
vA <- rowVars(ex$A[, , 5]);  vB <- rowVars(ex$B[, , 5])
vp <- ((Nt - 1) * vA + (Nt - 1) * vB) / (2 * Nt - 2)
t2_pooled <- (mB - mA)^2 / (vp * (1 / Nt + 1 / Nt))

max(abs(t2_uni - t2_pooled))   # expect a value near zero
```

## Observations

Both checks pass. The F statistic from `hotelling_t2()` and from `DescTools::HotellingsT2Test` agree at 2.833633, and in the one-electrode case the largest discrepancy from the pooled-variance squared t is 1.4e-14, which is machine precision. The statistic behaves as intended and the onsets below can be read.

# The T-squared time course

## Description

With the statistic verified, T-squared is computed at all 251 time points of the same simulated experiment used for the checks above, and plotted beside the virtual electrode from `simulation.qmd`, the maximum squared t across electrodes. The two are on different scales, so each is shown as a proportion of its own maximum.

## Justification

The shape of the curve that the onset methods will be given is examined before any onset is estimated. The quantity of interest is the baseline: how flat each curve is before 160 ms, and how sharply it leaves that baseline, since a statistic with a noisier baseline produces earlier false onsets whichever method reads it.

Scaling each curve by its own maximum makes the shapes comparable, but it also limits what the comparison can settle. Flatness then means flatness relative to the peak, so a statistic with a large peak appears to have a quiet baseline even where its absolute variability is high. What matters operationally is each curve's baseline relative to its own null distribution, which is what the permutation threshold and the FDR correction in the next section address directly. This figure is therefore read as evidence about shape, not as a verdict on either method.

## Code

```{r}
t2_mv <- hotelling_t2(ex$A, ex$B)

# the univariate comparison needs the Welch test from simulation.qmd
welch_t2p <- function(Ae, Be){
  nA <- ncol(Ae); nB <- ncol(Be)
  mA <- rowMeans(Ae); mB <- rowMeans(Be)
  vA <- rowVars(Ae);  vB <- rowVars(Be)
  se2  <- vA / nA + vB / nB
  tval <- (mB - mA) / sqrt(se2)
  df   <- se2^2 / ((vA / nA)^2 / (nA - 1) + (vB / nB)^2 / (nB - 1))
  list(t2 = tval^2, p = 2 * pt(-abs(tval), df))
}

# squared t at each electrode, then the maximum
T2obs <- sapply(1:9, function(e) welch_t2p(ex$A[, , e], ex$B[, , e])$t2)
t2_virtual <- apply(T2obs, 1, max)

curves <- tibble(time = Xf,
                 `Hotelling T2 (9 electrodes)` = t2_mv / max(t2_mv, na.rm = TRUE),
                 `max squared t (virtual electrode)` = t2_virtual / max(t2_virtual)) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "statistic", values_to = "value")
```

## Figure

```{r}
#| label: fig-curves
#| fig-cap: "The two ways of reducing nine electrodes to one time course, each scaled by its own maximum. The light-grey long-dashed line marks the true onset at 160 ms."
ggplot(curves, aes(time, value, linetype = statistic)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#ffffff") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_onset, linetype = "longdash", colour = "#c7c7c7", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(
    "Hotelling T2 (9 electrodes)" = "solid",
    "max squared t (virtual electrode)" = "longdash"
  )) +
  labs(x = "Time (ms)", y = "Statistic (proportion of its maximum)", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_dark_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Observations

Both statistics remain low through the pre-onset window and rise steeply after it, peaking near the peak of the template at 250 ms. Neither baseline is visibly quieter than the other on this scaling, which is the limitation set out above: the comparison is of shape, and the operative question is each curve against its own null distribution. The next section addresses that directly.

# Onsets from the T-squared curve

## Description

The curve is a single time course, so the three families of method from `simulation.qmd` apply directly, with no summary across electrodes needed:

- FDR, Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli, across time points, using the
  exact F transformation of T-squared to obtain a p-value at each time point, then
  the first significant point.
- MAX correction, taking the 95th percentile of the permutation distribution of
  the largest T-squared across time, then the first crossing.
- change point on the T-squared curve, by binary segmentation as implemented in
  the `changepoint` package (Killick & Eckley, 2014).

## Justification

The search space has shrunk. In `simulation.qmd` the FDR and MAX corrections cover 251 time points times nine electrodes; here the electrodes are inside the statistic, so the correction covers 251 time points only, and a smaller search space means a less severe correction. That gain is not free: the multivariate statistic spends nine degrees of freedom where a single electrode spends one, so its sensitivity at any given time point is lower than that of the strongest electrode. Which effect dominates is an empirical question.

The permutation is also harder to get wrong. In the univariate case one shared shuffle has to be applied deliberately across all electrodes, since electrodes are correlated and the resampling must not break that structure. Here a trial is a nine-element vector, so permuting trial labels moves the whole vector at once and the structure is preserved by construction.

Benjamini-Yekutieli is reported alongside Benjamini-Hochberg for the same reason as in `simulation.qmd`: adjacent time points are strongly dependent, and BY remains valid under arbitrary dependence where BH does not.

## Code

```{r}
nperm       <- 1000      # permutations for the MAX threshold, low on purpose:
                        # see the note on cost below
cpd_penalty <- "MBIC"   # change point penalty
sig_level   <- 0.05     # significance level for the FDR methods

# helpers that turn a time course into an onset in ms
cp_onset <- function(series, penalty = cpd_penalty){
  tryCatch({
    cp  <- cpt.meanvar(series, method = "BinSeg", Q = 2, penalty = penalty, minseglen = 2)
    pts <- cpts(cp)
    # earliest of the two change points, whatever order cpts() returns them in
    if(length(pts) == 0) NA_real_ else Xf[min(pts)]
  }, error = function(e) NA_real_)
}
first_cross <- function(series, thr){
  s <- which(series > thr); if(length(s) == 0) NA_real_ else Xf[s[1]]
}
first_sig <- function(pcol, level = sig_level){
  s <- which(pcol < level); if(length(s) == 0) NA_real_ else Xf[s[1]]
}

# onsets from one T2 curve, given the arrays it came from
mv_onsets <- function(A, B, nperm = nperm){
  nf <- dim(A)[1]; nA <- dim(A)[2]; nB <- dim(B)[2]; p <- dim(A)[3]

  t2 <- hotelling_t2(A, B)
  pv <- hotelling_p(t2, nA, nB, p)

  # permutation null: shuffle trial labels, keeping each trial's nine values
  # together, and save the largest T2 across time
  pool <- array(0, dim = c(nf, nA + nB, p))
  pool[, 1:nA, ]              <- A
  pool[, (nA + 1):(nA + nB), ] <- B

  null_max <- numeric(nperm)
  for(b in 1:nperm){
    perm <- sample(nA + nB)
    null_max[b] <- max(hotelling_t2(pool[, perm[1:nA], , drop = FALSE],
                                    pool[, perm[(nA + 1):(nA + nB)], , drop = FALSE]),
                       na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  thr <- quantile(null_max, 0.95, names = FALSE)

  tibble(method = c("Hotelling FDR BH", "Hotelling FDR BY",
                    "Hotelling MAX", "Hotelling CPD"),
         onset  = c(first_sig(p.adjust(pv, "BH")),
                    first_sig(p.adjust(pv, "BY")),
                    first_cross(t2, thr),
                    cp_onset(t2)))
}
```

## Table

```{r}
#| label: tbl-once-mv
#| tbl-cap: "Onset (ms) from the Hotelling T-squared curve, one simulated experiment, by each of the four methods."
set.seed(11)
mv_onsets(ex$A, ex$B, nperm = nperm) |> knitr::kable()
```

## Observations

On this run Benjamini-Hochberg returns 2 ms, the first time point of the epoch, which is a false positive rather than an estimate. Benjamini-Yekutieli gives 194 ms, the MAX threshold 204 ms and change point 178 ms, all later than the true 160 ms. Benjamini-Yekutieli is later than Benjamini-Hochberg, as its more conservative correction implies.


## Worked example

The four multivariate estimators can be read from the same Hotelling T-squared time course.

```{r}
#| label: fig-report-hotelling-strategies
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Worked example of the four Hotelling-based onset estimators. Light-grey long-dashed lines mark the true onset and white solid lines the returned onset, light-grey dotted lines the MAX threshold, and white bars corrected significant timepoints."
#| fig-alt: "Four dark-background panels show Hotelling BH, BY, MAX and CPD on one T-squared curve. The true onset and MAX threshold are light grey with distinct line types, while returned onsets and corrected significant-timepoint bars are white."

t2_ex_nb <- hotelling_t2(ex$A, ex$B)
p_ex_nb <- hotelling_p(t2_ex_nb, dim(ex$A)[2], dim(ex$B)[2], dim(ex$A)[3])
bh_ex_nb <- p.adjust(p_ex_nb, "BH")
by_ex_nb <- p.adjust(p_ex_nb, "BY")

set.seed(2604)
nA_nb <- dim(ex$A)[2]
nB_nb <- dim(ex$B)[2]
pool_nb <- array(0, dim = c(length(Xf), nA_nb + nB_nb, 9))
pool_nb[, 1:nA_nb, ] <- ex$A
pool_nb[, (nA_nb + 1):(nA_nb + nB_nb), ] <- ex$B
null_nb <- numeric(nperm)
for(b in seq_len(nperm)){
  perm <- sample(nA_nb + nB_nb)
  null_nb[b] <- max(
    hotelling_t2(
      pool_nb[, perm[1:nA_nb], , drop = FALSE],
      pool_nb[, perm[(nA_nb + 1):(nA_nb + nB_nb)], , drop = FALSE]
    ),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}
thr_nb <- quantile(null_nb, 0.95, names = FALSE)

methods_nb <- c("Hotelling BH", "Hotelling BY", "Hotelling MAX", "Hotelling CPD")
onsets_nb <- tibble(
  method = factor(methods_nb, levels = methods_nb),
  onset = c(
    first_sig(bh_ex_nb),
    first_sig(by_ex_nb),
    first_cross(t2_ex_nb, thr_nb),
    cp_onset(t2_ex_nb)
  )
)

trace_nb <- crossing(
  tibble(time = Xf, t2 = t2_ex_nb),
  method = factor(methods_nb, levels = methods_nb)
)

sig_nb <- bind_rows(
  tibble(time = Xf[bh_ex_nb < sig_level], method = "Hotelling BH"),
  tibble(time = Xf[by_ex_nb < sig_level], method = "Hotelling BY")
) |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = methods_nb),
         y = -0.05 * max(t2_ex_nb, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(trace_nb, aes(time, t2)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#ffffff", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(
    data = sig_nb,
    aes(x = time - 1, xend = time + 1, y = y, yend = y),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#ffffff",
    linewidth = 1.7, lineend = "butt"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    data = tibble(method = factor("Hotelling MAX", levels = methods_nb),
                  threshold = thr_nb),
    aes(yintercept = threshold), colour = "#c7c7c7",
    linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_onset, colour = "#c7c7c7",
             linetype = "longdash", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(
    data = onsets_nb |> filter(!is.na(onset)),
    aes(xintercept = onset), colour = "#ffffff",
    linetype = "solid", linewidth = 0.75
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~method, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.10, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = "Time (ms)", y = expression(T^2)) +
  theme_dark_bw() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(colour = "#ffffff", face = "bold"))
```

# Simulation results (10,000 iterations)

## Description

One experiment says little, so performance is evaluated over 10,000 Monte Carlo iterations with 50 trials per condition. The completed simulation is loaded from the saved result file rather than regenerated when this notebook is rendered.

## Justification

Using the saved production run keeps the analysis reproducible without repeating the computationally expensive permutation simulation during rendering. The four methods are therefore evaluated from the same 10,000 completed multivariate experiments.

## Code

```{r}
# Load the completed multivariate simulation output.
mv_file <- if(file.exists("data/simres_n50_mult.RData")) {
  "data/simres_n50_mult.RData"
} else {
  "simres_n50_mult.RData"
}

load(mv_file)

# Standardise the saved result table if necessary.
if(exists("sim_mv")) {
  sim_mv <- as_tibble(sim_mv)
} else {
  objs <- mget(ls(), inherits = FALSE)
  hits <- objs[vapply(objs, function(x)
    is.data.frame(x) &&
      all(c("iter", "method", "onset") %in% names(x)), logical(1))]
  if(length(hits) != 1) stop("Could not identify the saved multivariate result table.")
  sim_mv <- as_tibble(hits[[1]])
}

stopifnot(max(sim_mv$iter, na.rm = TRUE) == 10000)

mv_methods <- c("Hotelling FDR BH", "Hotelling FDR BY",
                "Hotelling MAX", "Hotelling CPD")

sim_mv <- sim_mv |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = mv_methods))

method_summary_mv <- sim_mv |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(
    median_onset = median(onset, na.rm = TRUE),
    bias = round(median_onset - true_onset, 1),
    mae = round(mean(abs(onset - true_onset), na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    sd_onset = round(sd(onset, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    underestimation = round(100 * mean(onset < true_onset, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(onset)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}

method_summary_mv |>
  rename(
    `Method` = method,
    `Median onset (ms)` = median_onset,
    `Bias (ms)` = bias,
    `MAE (ms)` = mae,
    `SD (ms)` = sd_onset,

#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Bias and mean absolute error across the six primary and four Hotelling-based strategies. Primary and multivariate strategies are distinguished by point shape."
#| fig-alt: "Dark-background scatter plot comparing signed bias and mean absolute error for ten strategies. Six primary strategies and four Hotelling strategies use different point shapes, with a light-grey dotted vertical line at zero bias."

# Load the completed univariate main run solely for this cross-family comparison.
univ_file_nb <- if(file.exists("data/simres_n50.RData")) {
  "data/simres_n50.RData"
} else {
  "simres_n50.RData"
}

env_nb <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
load(univ_file_nb, envir = env_nb)
obj_nb <- as.list(env_nb)

pick_nb <- function(required, forbidden = character()){
  hit <- obj_nb[vapply(obj_nb, function(x)
    is.data.frame(x) &&
      all(required %in% names(x)) &&
      !any(forbidden %in% names(x)), logical(1))]
  if(length(hit) != 1) stop("Could not identify saved univariate table in ", univ_file_nb)
  as_tibble(hit[[1]])
}

pe_nb <- if("perelec_all" %in% names(obj_nb)) {
  as_tibble(obj_nb[["perelec_all"]])
} else {
  pick_nb(c("iter", "electrode", "weight", "method", "onset"))
}
vi_nb <- if("virtual_all" %in% names(obj_nb)) {
  as_tibble(obj_nb[["virtual_all"]])
} else {
  pick_nb(c("iter", "method", "onset"), c("electrode", "weight"))
}

safe_min_nb <- function(x){
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if(length(x) == 0) NA_real_ else min(x)
}
safe_q_nb <- function(x, p){
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if(length(x) == 0) NA_real_ else quantile(x, p, names = FALSE)
}

group_nb <- pe_nb |>
  group_by(iter, method) |>
  summarise(
    min = safe_min_nb(onset),
    median = safe_q_nb(onset, 0.50),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(min, median), names_to = "summary", values_to = "onset") |>
  bind_rows(vi_nb |> transmute(iter, method, summary = "single", onset))

spec_nb <- tribble(
  ~method, ~summary, ~strategy,
  "FDR BH", "min", "BH min",
  "FDR BY", "min", "BY min",
  "MAX across", "min", "MAX min",
  "CPD per electrode", "median", "CPD median",
  "CPD if MAX significant", "min", "CPD MAX-selected min",
  "CPD virtual", "single", "Pooled CPD"
)

primary_cmp_nb <- group_nb |>
  inner_join(spec_nb, by = c("method", "summary")) |>
  group_by(strategy) |>
  summarise(
    bias = median(onset, na.rm = TRUE) - true_onset,
    mae = mean(abs(onset - true_onset), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(family = "Primary methods", label = strategy)

hot_cmp_nb <- sim_mv |>
  filter(!is.na(onset)) |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(
    bias = median(onset) - true_onset,
    mae = mean(abs(onset - true_onset)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    family = "Hotelling methods",
    label = recode(as.character(method),
                   "Hotelling FDR BH" = "Hotelling BH",
                   "Hotelling FDR BY" = "Hotelling BY",
                   "Hotelling MAX" = "Hotelling MAX",
                   "Hotelling CPD" = "Hotelling CPD")
  )

cmp_nb <- bind_rows(primary_cmp_nb, hot_cmp_nb) |>
  mutate(family = factor(family, levels = c("Primary methods", "Hotelling methods")))

ggplot(cmp_nb, aes(bias, mae, shape = family)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#c7c7c7",
             linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.65) +
  geom_point(size = 3.2, stroke = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label),
            colour = "#ffffff", size = 2.9,
            nudge_y = -2.5, check_overlap = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Primary methods" = 16, "Hotelling methods" = 17)) +
  labs(x = "Bias (ms)", y = "Mean absolute error (ms)",
       shape = NULL) +
  theme_dark_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(8, 14, 8, 8))
```

## Observations

Across 10,000 simulations, Hotelling BH had the smallest median bias among the four multivariate procedures, with a median onset of 180 ms and a bias of +20 ms, but its distribution was broad: MAE was 53.5 ms, SD was 65.7 ms, and 39.7% of estimates occurred before 160 ms. Hotelling BY was later, with a median onset of 196 ms, bias of +36 ms, MAE of 41.4 ms, SD of 38.0 ms, and 8.8% underestimation. Hotelling MAX had a median onset of 202 ms and bias of +42 ms; its MAE was 43.7 ms, SD 20.8 ms, and underestimation 1.9%. Hotelling CPD gave the lowest MAE and smallest SD of the four multivariate procedures, with a median onset of 186 ms, bias of +26 ms, MAE of 26.5 ms, SD of 11.4 ms, and 1.6% underestimation. All four methods returned an onset in all 10,000 simulations.

# Discussion and next steps

This simulation is not built to favour the multivariate test, and two features of it work directly against the test. Both belong in any reading of the results.

The first is the noise. Hotelling's T-squared earns its advantage over separate univariate tests by using the covariance between electrodes: when the noise is correlated across electrodes but the effect is not, the test can separate the two. In this simulation the noise is generated independently at every electrode, so the true covariance matrix is close to diagonal and there is little structure for the test to exploit. What it estimates instead is sampling noise in a nine by nine matrix, from 100 trials. The design was chosen in the demo as the harder case for the univariate methods, but it is also the case in which the multivariate test has least to offer. A version with noise shared across neighbouring electrodes would be a fairer test of it, and is the obvious follow-up.

The second is dilution. Four of the nine electrodes carry no signal at all. Hotelling's T-squared spends degrees of freedom on all nine dimensions regardless, so those four contribute variance without contributing effect, and the statistic is weaker than it would be with only the five signal electrodes. This is the same electrode-selection problem as in `simulation.qmd`, arriving from a different direction: there it decided which onsets to summarise, here it decides which dimensions enter the test. The remedies are the same, an a priori region of interest or a data-driven selection step, and neither is free.

Against those disadvantages sits one clear advantage: the correction covers 251 time points instead of 251 times nine, and the permutation cannot break the correlation structure, since it moves whole trials. Comparable performance in a design tilted against the test would therefore be a stronger result than the raw numbers suggest.

Next steps:

- fold the T-squared curve into `simulation.qmd` as four further strategies, so that the
  multivariate and univariate methods are compared on the same runs rather than
  across notebooks.
- repeat with noise shared across neighbouring electrodes, which is the case the
  multivariate test is designed for.
- try a linear discriminant analysis across electrodes as an alternative
  multivariate statistic, which does not rest on a common covariance in the same
  way.
- test the effect of restricting the test to a subset of electrodes, to separate
  the dilution problem from the noise problem.
